stumbles.quote: Jev had done well on routing questions, so I was hopeful.
stumbles.why: Refers to earlier Jev evaluations on routing questions that the text never describes.
Oskar is never introduced, so his role is unclear.
The tool is never explained. The reader can't tell what it checks or what a 'tic' is.
register.md and the definitions in it are never explained, and the text doesn't say which tic it means.

stumbles.quote: at a 5% error budget it could settle only 24.5% of hits
stumbles.why: 'Settle' and 'error budget' are not defined. The text doesn't say what settling a hit means or what the 5% measures.

stumbles.quote: The bar set in advance was 50%.
stumbles.why: The text doesn't say who set the bar or why it is 50%.

stumbles.quote: A reviewer would still have to read three of every four hits
stumbles.why: This is roughly consistent with 24.5% settled, but it is stated as an approximation without saying so.

stumbles.quote: The category baseline already captures most of that difference without a model call, which explains why it comes so close to Jev on ranking.
stumbles.why: The baseline scored 0.769 against Jev's 0.808, and it beat Jev on accuracy. 'Comes so close' glosses over this. The with-definition and without-definition Jev numbers are also easy to mix up.
The table counts (5+5+16 of 105 hits) don't match the 261 agreed hits or the 35.2% real-tic rate. The text doesn't say whether the table covers a different set or only some rules.

point: Jev, a small probability model, settled only 24.5% of lint hits against a 50% bar, so it won't be used in post review, and the plan is to tighten the lint's weak triad and participle rules instead.
